title: An exact algorithm for U(N) matrix models in the gauge-invariant singlet sector
abstract: Matrix models appear as fundamental descriptions of M-theory and D-brane dynamics, and via the gauge/gravity duality their gauge-invariant, or singlet, sector describes the purely gravitational degrees of freedom in the holographic dual. We present a new exact algorithm for computing observables of bosonic U(N) matrix models in the gauge-invariant singlet sector. This sector is spanned by an orthogonal basis of Schur polynomials (for a single matrix) and restricted Schur polynomials (for multiple matrices), which diagonalizes the free Hamiltonian and provides a natural truncation of the Hilbert space by excitation number. Matrix elements of the interaction Hamiltonian, or any gauge-invariant observable, are evaluated through a group-theoretic reduction to cosets and double cosets of suitable subgroups of the symmetric group, together with character sums on the symmetric group. The resulting entries are closed-form polynomials in the gauge-group rank N, assembled from group-theoretic data that are precomputed once and can be reused for any N and any coupling constants. We validate the one-matrix implementation against the exact mapping to N non-interacting fermions, demonstrating rapid convergence of the low-lying spectrum with the cutoff. The multi-matrix extension is outlined; its main bottleneck is the computation of restricted characters of the symmetric group, for which no algorithm comparable to the Murnaghan--Nakayama rule is currently known. The framework gives direct access to finite-N, finite-coupling dynamics of gauge-invariant states and opens a new computational window on the non-planar regime of holographic matrix models.
summary: This paper introduces an exact, group-theoretically derived algorithm for calculating observables in U(N) matrix models within their physically relevant gauge-invariant sector. By mapping the problem onto representations of the symmetric group, it provides explicit polynomial formulas for finite-N dynamics. This opens a new computational window into non-planar regimes of holographic quantum gravity models.
main_problem: The primary goal is developing an exact, systematic algorithm for computing observables within the gauge-invariant singlet sector of bosonic U(N) matrix models.
main_result: The authors present a group-theoretic framework that yields closed-form polynomial expressions in N for these matrix elements, allowing access to finite-N dynamics previously difficult to compute.
method: The method relies on decomposing the Hilbert space using Schur polynomials and evaluating matrix elements via group-theoretic reductions involving cosets and character sums of the symmetric group.
model_or_system: The system is a bosonic U(N) matrix model, fundamental in describing M-theory and D-brane dynamics through the gauge/gravity duality. The Hamiltonian involves quadratic and quartic terms in the matrices.
key_observables: Hamiltonian matrix elements, correlation functions of gauge-invariant observables (singlets), and the low-lying energy spectrum.
important_parameters: The rank N of the gauge group, the coupling constant g, and the mass parameter m.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to the gauge-invariant singlet sector. A major limitation noted is the difficulty in computing restricted characters for multi-matrix extensions.
figures_summary: Not specified by detailed notes; general structure involves mathematical derivations related to tensor decomposition and group theory.
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the physical context (M-theory/D-branes) to defining the singlet basis using Schur polynomials, deriving explicit formulas for gauge generators, calculating correlators via Wick's theorem, and finally presenting the general algorithm structure.
why_interesting: While highly abstract, the techniques developed—using representation theory (Schur functions, symmetric groups) to solve complex many-body quantum field theories in a finite-N limit—are analogous to advanced methods used in strongly correlated electron systems or lattice gauge theories.
